title: The two-minute drill: the clock, field-goal range and the onside kick
html:
Why this lesson now: the Film Room mirror (football-brief, branch film-room) was checked this morning: it still holds only one logged game (Eagles at Bears, Week 3, 0 saved snaps) and no review files, and the original football-film-room repository was again not reachable from this run (access denied: not configured for this session). So there's no new miss of yours to fix, and no snap of yours this connects to yet. This lesson takes a new concept from Thursday night, where 30 of the 54 points that beat the brief's Under came in two short windows: the last 14 seconds of the first half and the last 94 seconds of the game.

The big idea: at the end of each half, football changes. The team with the ball isn't trying to have a "good drive" anymore; it's trying to score before the clock hits 0:00, or to keep the other team from getting the ball back. Three things run the end of every half: the clock, field-goal range and, at the end of a game, the onside kick.

Top: the kick math, using Thursday's two late field goals (white dot = line of scrimmage, yellow dot = the hold). Middle: the end of the first half on a timeline. Bottom: what stops the game clock.

  1. Field-goal range (diagram, part 1). A field goal is kicked from 7 yards behind the line of scrimmage, and the goalposts sit at the back of the 10-yard end zone. So the kick is always the yard line + 17. Cairo Santos's ball was snapped at New England's 41: 41 + 10 + 7 = 58 yards, the longest of his career, with 1:34 left, after he'd missed from 53 earlier. NFL.com said a kick like that had about a 27.6% chance. Most NFL kickers are reliable inside about 50 yards (the opponent's 33), which is why a two-minute drive is aimed at "getting into range" first and a touchdown second. New England's answer, Andy Borregales from 47 (the Chicago 30), came with 37 seconds left.
  2. The clock (part 3). In the last two minutes the offense lives on plays that stop the clock: an incomplete pass, a run or catch that goes out of bounds, a timeout, or a spike (the quarterback throws the ball straight into the ground on purpose, an incomplete pass that stops the clock without using a timeout). The NFL adds the two-minute warning. In college the clock also stops briefly after a first down, but only in the last two minutes of each half. A completed pass in the middle of the field keeps the clock running, which is why receivers race for the sideline.
  3. Points in a hurry (part 2). Chicago scored with 14 seconds left in the half (Luther Burden, 24 yards) to go up 20-7. That should have ended the half. Instead, after the kickoff, New England got one more snap, and Rhamondre Stevenson caught Drake Maye's pass and went 48 yards for a touchdown on the final play: 20-14. Fourteen seconds, 14 points. This is how totals go over in a hurry (Market 101, Lesson 9).
  4. The onside kick. A team that's behind late can kick off short, hoping to recover the ball itself after it travels at least 10 yards. In the NFL it rarely works, and the kicking team has to announce it under the current kickoff rules. After Borregales's field goal cut it to 30-24 with 37 seconds left, New England tried one; Rome Odunze recovered it for Chicago, and that ended it.
  5. College overtime (a bonus, two games went there Thursday). App State-James Madison and Memphis-East Carolina both went to overtime. In college, each team gets a possession starting at the opponent's 25; from the third overtime on, teams just run alternating two-point plays. That's why college overtime points pile up fast, and why Kalshi totals, which count overtime (Lesson 25), can jump at the end.

How to log it in your drill: in a two-minute drill the offense is almost always passing: log PASS unless you see a clear handoff. A spike is a PASS (it's an intentional incompletion). A kneel-down (the quarterback takes the snap and drops to one knee) is a RUN by the stat sheet; it's the one end-of-game call you can make with certainty before the snap: the leading team in victory formation, everyone bunched tight around the quarterback.

Real examples to look for this weekend: the end of the first half in Indiana at Michigan (Sun 1:00 a.m. JST / Sat 9:00 a.m. PT, FOX): does Michigan, with a freshman quarterback, try to score or run out the clock? And on Sunday, watch for teams at the opponent's 35–40 with under a minute left: that's the line where coaches decide between one more pass and a long field goal.

Video: search YouTube for "two minute drill explained," "how field goal distance is calculated," and "onside kick rules NFL 2026," then watch the last 14 seconds of the first half of Patriots-Bears.

Practice it in Football Camp → (Station 6: Situations)

quiz.q: The ball is snapped at the opponent's 35. How long is the field-goal try?
Which of these does NOT stop the clock?
o: A catch in the middle of the field, tackled in bounds
quiz.w: A completed pass where the receiver is tackled in bounds keeps the clock running. That's why receivers fight to reach the sideline late in a half.

quiz.q: In your drill, the quarterback takes the snap and throws it straight into the ground to stop the clock. How do you log it?
quiz.w: A spike is an intentional incomplete pass, so it's a PASS. A kneel-down is the opposite: a RUN.

quiz.q: In college overtime, where does each possession start?
quiz.w: Each team starts at the opponent's 25. From the third overtime on, teams alternate two-point tries instead.
